intro: Devon stares at a two-page article about honeybees and wants to give up. Twenty minutes later he can say the whole thing in two sentences, and he did not copy one word. Priya reads two articles about the same tornado and sees that one is built like a clock and the other like a chain of arrows. A class opens a dusty yearbook and learns something true about their own school that nobody in the building knew.

This unit is about reading to learn: articles, science pages, history pages, charts, maps and websites. You will find the main idea and the details that hold it up. You will spot the five shapes a text can take and take notes that match. You will read a chart like a paragraph, tell a fact from an opinion, and tell a primary source from a secondary one.

By the end, you will be able to take a real question nobody can answer, find good sources, take honest notes, and write an answer with evidence. That is what scientists, reporters and historians do every day. It starts with one sentence in an article that all the others hold up.
bigQuestion: How do you read a text you did not choose and come away knowing something true?

timeline.t: Skim the title, headings and pictures and ask what you want to find out.
Read a paragraph and find the sentence the others hold up: the main idea.
Sort the details that support the idea from the sentences that are just extra.
Read the captions, diagrams, maps and sidebars as part of the text.
Spot the shape: sequence, description, compare, cause and effect, or problem and solution.
Take notes in the shape of the text: a list, two columns, or boxes with arrows.
Read a second text on the same topic and compare what each one keeps and leaves out.
Ask a research question that is specific and that nobody in the room can answer yet.
Find primary and secondary sources, judge which are reliable, and note where each fact came from.
Write the answer in your own words, back it with evidence, and say what is still unknown.

words.d: the most important point a text makes about its topic
a fact, example or reason that supports the main idea
a short retelling of the main idea and biggest details in your own words
to figure out something the text does not say, using clues
the words under or beside a picture that explain it
the way a text is built: sequence, description, compare and contrast, cause and effect, or problem and solution
a word that hints at a text's shape, like first, both, because or solved
the reason something happens
something made at the time of an event by a person who was there
something made later by a person who studied the event
what a person thinks or feels; it cannot be proved true or false
using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own

test.q: "Honeybees" is a topic. Which of these is a main idea?
choices: A honeybee hive works like a busy city
test.why: A main idea is a whole sentence that makes a point about the topic.

test.q: What do supporting details do for a main idea?
choices: Hold it up like table legs
test.why: Details are facts, examples and reasons that prove the main idea.

test.q: Which is a real summary of a paragraph?
choices: The main idea and biggest details in your own words
test.why: A summary is short and in your own words.

test.q: "Maya grabbed her umbrella and boots." The rain is...
test.why: The text never says rain, but the clues point to it.

test.q: Where is a key term's meaning often found on a page?
test.why: Writers bold a key term and often define it in the same sentence.

test.q: You need one date from a long article. Which way of reading is fastest?
test.why: Scanning hunts for one specific thing like a number.

test.q: "First the sky turned green. Next the sirens sounded. Then the funnel touched down." What shape is this?
test.why: First, next, then: events in time order.

test.q: "Warm air rose, so the storm began to spin." Which is the effect?
test.why: The spinning is the result of the rising air.

test.q: Which note shape fits a compare-and-contrast text?
test.why: Two columns put two things side by side.

test.q: The sirens sounded and then the funnel touched down. Did the sirens cause the funnel?
choices: No, close in time is not cause
test.why: Two events close together are not always cause and effect.

test.q: Which is a primary source about a school's opening day in 1959?
choices: A letter written that day by a student
test.why: The letter was made at the time by someone who was there.

test.q: "The playground has three slides." Fact or opinion?
choices: Opinion, because it is about a playground
Fact, because you can count the slides
test.why: It can be checked by counting, so it is a fact.

test.q: Which research question is the right size?
choices: What is everything about the ocean?
Why did our town build a wall of rocks along the lake?
test.why: It is specific, sources can answer it, and you cannot just look.

test.q: You want to keep a source's exact words in your notes. What do you do?
choices: Put quotation marks around them and note the source
Write them in a different color
test.why: Quotation marks are a promise that the words are not yours.

test.q: Which website is most reliable for a school-history question?
choices: One with no author and flashing ads
One about a different school in another state
One that says it is the best site ever
The town's official site with a date and a contact
test.why: You can tell who made it and when, and you can check it.

write.prompt: Pick one of the two tornado articles from Chapter 15. Claim which one would help a new student understand tornadoes better. Use evidence about how each article is built, and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: name the article and say it is the better one for a new student.
Evidence: describe its shape (sequence or cause and effect) and one thing it includes that the other leaves out.
Reasoning: explain why that shape and those facts help someone who knows nothing about tornadoes.
The other side: say one thing the other article does well, then explain why your choice still wins.

title: Reading to Learn

chapters.title: Main Idea and Details
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you find the one thing an article most wants you to know?

story.title: The Sentence That Holds the Hive Together
story.kicker: A class reads an article about honeybees, and one student finds the sentence that every other sentence leans on.
paragraphs: Mr. Bell hands out an article called "A City in a Box." It is about honeybees. Devon groans. It is two whole pages. There are words like colony and nectar. "Read the first paragraph," Mr. Bell says. "Then stop. Find the sentence that the other sentences hold up."

Devon reads. One sentence says a hive can hold many thousands of bees. Another says every bee has a job. Another says worker bees fly out to flowers and bring back nectar. Another says guard bees stand at the door. Devon frowns. Which one is the big one?

Then he sees it. The second sentence says, "A honeybee hive works like a busy city, and every bee has a job." The nectar sentence is a job. The guard sentence is a job. The thousands of bees are the people of the city. Every other sentence is an example of that one.

"That's the main idea," Devon says out loud. Mr. Bell nods. "The rest are details. They hold it up like legs hold up a table." Devon reads the second page. It has a heading, a picture of a waggle dance, and a caption. Now the two pages do not feel so long.

Before the bell, Mr. Bell asks the class to say the whole article in two sentences. Devon writes: "A hive is like a city where each bee has a job. Workers gather nectar, guards protect the door, and the queen lays the eggs." He did not copy one line. He got it.
story.think: Devon found the main idea by asking which sentence the others held up. Where else could you use that question?

lessons.title: The Topic Is Not the Point
lessons.mainIdea: The topic is what a text is about in a word or two; the main idea is what the text says about that topic.
reading: Read this short paragraph. "Dogs need a walk every day. A walk keeps a dog's legs strong. It lets the dog sniff and see new things. A dog that walks is calmer at home." What is it about? Dogs. That is the *topic*. The topic is just the subject, one or two words.

Now ask a harder question. What does the paragraph say about dogs? It says dogs need a walk every day. That is the *main idea*. The main idea is a whole sentence. It is the point the writer wants you to walk away with.

Here is a quick test. If your answer is one word, you found the topic. If your answer is a sentence with a verb, you found the main idea. "Honeybees" is a topic. "A honeybee hive works like a busy city" is a main idea.

words.d: the subject of a text, said in one or two words
the most important point a text makes about its topic, said in a sentence

look.title: Two Answers for One Paragraph
look.text: Picture a paragraph about the school lunchroom. It says the lunchroom is loud. It says four hundred kids eat there at once. It says the tables are close together. It says the tile floor bounces every sound. A student says the topic is "the lunchroom." Another says the main idea is "The lunchroom is loud because so many kids eat in a hard, crowded room."
look.prompt: Why is the second answer a main idea and the first answer only a topic?

check.q: What is a topic?
choices: The last sentence of a text
The subject of a text in a word or two
A fact that proves the point
check.why: The topic is just the subject, like dogs or honeybees. It is not a whole point.

check.q: Which one is a main idea, not a topic?
choices: Dogs need a walk every day
check.why: A main idea is a whole sentence that makes a point. The other three are one- or two-word topics.

check.q: You answer with a single word. What did you most likely find?
check.why: One word is a topic. A main idea needs a sentence with a verb.

lessons.title: Details Hold Up the Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Supporting details are the facts, examples and reasons that prove or explain the main idea.
reading: Think of a table. The top is the main idea. The legs are the *details*. "A honeybee hive works like a busy city." That is the top. "Workers gather nectar. Guards stand at the door. The queen lays eggs." Those are the legs. Take the legs away and the top falls.

A detail can be a fact, an example, a number or a reason. In the dog paragraph, "a walk keeps a dog's legs strong" is a reason. "It lets the dog sniff new things" is an example. Each one answers the question, "How do you know?"

Not every sentence is a detail. Some sentences are just extra. If a paragraph about bee jobs says, "Bees are yellow and black," that sentence does not hold up the idea. Good readers sort the legs from the extra.

words.d: a fact, example or reason that supports the main idea
to hold up or prove; details support the main idea

look.title: One Idea, Three Legs
look.text: Chicago winters are hard on sidewalks. Water gets into tiny cracks and freezes. Ice takes up more room than water, so the cracks get wider. Salt trucks help drivers, but salt eats into the concrete too. By spring, many blocks have new holes.
look.prompt: Which sentence is the main idea? Name two details that hold it up.

check.q: What do supporting details do?
choices: They prove or explain the main idea
check.why: Details are the legs that hold up the main idea. They answer, "How do you know?"

check.q: In the sidewalk paragraph, which sentence is a detail?
choices: Chicago winters are hard on sidewalks
Water gets into tiny cracks and freezes
check.why: The freezing water is a fact that shows how winter hurts sidewalks. The first choice is the main idea itself.

check.q: A paragraph is about bee jobs. Which sentence is extra, not a detail?
choices: Guard bees stand at the door
check.why: Color does not explain a bee's job. The other three sentences all hold up the idea about jobs.

lessons.title: The Main Idea of a Whole Article
lessons.mainIdea: A whole article has one main idea, and each paragraph's main idea is a detail that supports it.
reading: One paragraph has a main idea. A whole article has one too. Think of a bigger table. The article's main idea is the top. Each paragraph's main idea is a leg. The details in each paragraph are the small screws that hold each leg on.

Take the bee article. Paragraph one says every bee has a job. Paragraph two says the hive stays warm because bees shiver together. Paragraph three says bees dance to share where flowers are. Put them together: "Honeybees survive because they work as a team." That is the article's main idea.

To find it, read the title. Read the first and last paragraphs closely. Then ask what all the paragraph ideas have in common. The answer is often stated near the start or the end. Sometimes it is not stated at all, and you must build it yourself.

words.d: a short piece of nonfiction writing about one subject
shared by all; what several ideas have that is the same

look.title: Where Writers Put the Main Idea
look.cite: counted for this lesson, in ten short model articles written for this course
look.prompt: Based on these counts, where should you look first for an article's main idea?

check.q: How does a paragraph's main idea relate to the whole article?
choices: It is a detail that supports the article's main idea
It is always the same as the article's main idea
It has nothing to do with the article
check.why: Each paragraph's idea is a leg under the article's big idea.

check.q: Three paragraphs say bees have jobs, keep warm together, and dance to share news. What do they have in common?
check.why: Jobs, shivering together and dancing to share are all teamwork. That shared idea is the article's main idea.

check.q: Where is an article's main idea most often stated?
choices: Near the start or the end
check.why: Writers usually state the main idea early or in the closing. The middle mostly holds details.

lessons.title: A Summary in Your Own Words
lessons.mainIdea: A summary tells the main idea and the biggest details in a few sentences, in your words, not the author's.
reading: Devon said a two-page article in two sentences. That is a *summary*. A summary is short. It gives the main idea and the most important details. It leaves out the small stuff, the jokes and the repeats.

Here is the trap. Copying a sentence is not a summary. If you write the author's words, you did not show that you understood them. Close the book. Say the idea out loud to a friend. Then write what you said. Those are your own words.

Try it with this: "Sea otters float on their backs. They hold hands while they sleep so they do not drift apart. They also wrap themselves in kelp, a kind of seaweed." A summary: "Sea otters use holding hands and kelp to stay in place while they sleep." Short, true, and in your words.

words.d: a short retelling of the main idea and biggest details in your own words
a large brown seaweed that grows in the ocean

look.title: Copy or Summary?
look.text: Two students summarize the same paragraph about the moon. Ana writes: "The moon has no air, so there is no wind. The moon has no air, so footprints stay for a very long time." Luis writes: "Because the moon has no air or wind, marks on it last a very long time." The original paragraph had the exact sentence, "The moon has no air, so there is no wind."
look.prompt: Which student wrote a real summary? What did the other student do instead?

check.q: What belongs in a summary?
choices: The main idea and the biggest details
check.why: A summary is short and keeps only what matters most.

check.q: Why is copying a sentence not summarizing?
choices: The author's sentences are always wrong
It does not show you understood the idea
check.why: Putting the idea in your own words proves you understood it. Copying skips that step.

check.q: Which is the best trick for using your own words?
choices: Say the idea out loud with the book closed
Change one word in each sentence
check.why: When you say it aloud without looking, the words that come out are yours.

lessons.title: What It Says and What It Hints
lessons.mainIdea: A text says some things explicitly, right on the page, and implies other things that you must figure out from clues.
reading: Read this. "Maya grabbed her umbrella and her boots before she left for school." Does the sentence say it is raining? No. It says umbrella and boots. But you know. The text *implies* rain. To imply is to hint without saying.

Now read this. "It was raining hard, so Maya grabbed her umbrella." This time the text says it. It is *explicit*, right there in plain words. Good readers know the difference. When a teacher asks, "What does the text say?" she wants the explicit part. When she asks, "What can you tell?" she wants what it implies.

Check your hints against the words. If a text says a bee "shivers to make heat," you may infer bees can be cold. You cannot infer bees have fur. Nothing on the page points to that. A good inference always has a clue you can point to.

words.d: said plainly, right on the page
to hint at something without saying it directly
to figure out something the text does not say, using clues

look.title: Find the Hint
look.text: The bus was late again. Jamal checked his watch three times. He shifted his backpack from one shoulder to the other. When the bus finally came, he ran the last few steps and dropped into a seat with a long breath.
look.prompt: What does the text say explicitly about the bus? What does it imply about how Jamal feels?

check.q: A text says, "Maya grabbed her umbrella and boots." What is implied?
check.why: Umbrella plus boots are clues for rain. The text hints it without saying it.

check.q: What does explicit mean?
check.why: Explicit information is right there in the words, like "It was raining hard."

check.q: A text says bees shiver to make heat. Which inference is fair?
check.why: Shivering for heat points to cold. Nothing on the page points to fur, fear or snow.

sections.title: Reading the Parts of a Page

lessons.title: Headings and Bold Words
lessons.mainIdea: Headings tell you what a section is about, and bold words point to terms the author wants you to learn.
reading: Open a science book. The page is not one gray block. There is a big title. Under it are smaller titles, like "How Bees Find Flowers" or "Inside the Hive." Those are *headings*. A heading is a label for a chunk of text. It tells you the topic of that chunk before you read it.

Some words on the page are darker and thicker than the rest. They are in *bold*. Writers put a word in bold when it is a key term. Often the meaning is right there in the same sentence. "Bees carry *pollen*, a yellow dust from flowers, on their legs." The bold word plus the words after it give you a free definition.

Use these parts before you read. Run your eyes down the headings. Now you know the map of the article. Then read the bold words. Now you know the vocabulary. You have not read a full paragraph yet, and you already know a lot.

words.d: a short title above a section that tells what the section is about
dark, thick letters that make a key word stand out
a fine yellow dust that flowers make; bees carry it from flower to flower

look.title: A Map Made of Headings
look.text: An article about the Chicago River has these headings: "A River That Ran Backward," "Why the City Changed It," "The River Today." A student has not read one paragraph. But she says, "I bet this is about how people changed the river's direction, and what it is like now."
look.prompt: How could she guess the article's shape before reading it? Which heading would you read first if you wanted to know why the change happened?

check.q: What does a heading do?
choices: It tells the topic of the section under it
check.why: A heading is a label for the chunk of text below it.

check.q: Why do writers put a word in bold?
choices: Because it is a key term to learn
Because it is the longest word
check.why: Bold marks a key term, and its meaning is often given in the same sentence.

check.q: You read the headings and the bold words before reading the article. What do you gain?
choices: Nothing; you must read every word first
A map of the topics and the key vocabulary
check.why: Headings give the map; bold words give the vocabulary. Then the article is easier.

lessons.title: Captions, Diagrams, Maps and Sidebars
lessons.mainIdea: Pictures, diagrams, maps and sidebars carry facts that the paragraphs may not say, so read them as part of the text.
reading: Under the picture of the waggle dance is one line of small print: "A worker bee dances in a figure eight to show where flowers are." That is a *caption*. Many readers skip captions. That is a mistake. The caption often has a fact that is nowhere else on the page.

A *diagram* is a drawing with labels. A diagram of a bee might label the wings, the stinger and the pollen baskets on its legs. A map shows where. A map of Illinois might mark the towns with the most beekeepers. Read a map the way you read a sentence: look at the title, the labels and the key.

A *sidebar* is a box of text set off from the rest, often with its own color. It tells a small side story, like "How Honey Is Made." Sidebars are extra, but they are often the most interesting part. Read the picture, the caption, the diagram and the box. All of it is the text.

words.d: the words under or beside a picture that explain it
a drawing with labels that shows the parts of something
a box of extra text set off from the main article

look.title: Where the Facts Hide
look.cite: counted for this lesson, in a two-page model article on honeybees written for this course
look.prompt: How many facts would a reader miss by reading only the paragraphs? Is that a lot?

check.q: What is a caption?
choices: The words that explain a picture
check.why: A caption sits under or beside a picture and tells what it shows.

check.q: In the fact count, how many facts sit outside the paragraphs?
check.why: Captions (4) plus diagram labels (6) plus the sidebar (3) make 13 facts outside the paragraphs.

check.q: A student skips every diagram and caption. What happens?
choices: He reads faster and misses nothing
He misses facts that are only in those parts
He finds the main idea faster
check.why: Captions and diagrams often carry facts the paragraphs never state.

lessons.title: Skim First, Scan for Answers
lessons.mainIdea: Skimming means reading fast to get the general idea; scanning means moving your eyes to find one specific thing.
reading: You have two minutes and a four-page article. Do not start at word one. *Skim* it. Read the title, the headings, the first sentence of each paragraph, and the last paragraph. Your eyes move fast. You are looking for the big shape, not the small facts. In two minutes you know what the article is about.

Now the teacher asks, "How many eggs can a queen bee lay in a day?" You do not skim for that. You *scan*. Scanning is hunting for one thing. Your eyes jump down the page looking for a number, or the word "eggs," or the word "queen." You ignore everything else until you land on it.

Skim to learn the shape. Scan to find a fact. Read closely to understand. Good readers use all three, and they choose on purpose. If someone says, "Just find the date," scan. If someone says, "Tell me what this is about," skim, then read.

words.d: to read quickly to get the general idea
to move your eyes over a page looking for one specific word or fact

look.title: Two Jobs, Two Ways to Read
look.text: Rosa has a sheet with two jobs. Job one: "In one sentence, what is this article about?" Job two: "On what date did the beekeeper first open the hive?" For the first job she reads the title, the headings and the first sentence of each paragraph. For the second she runs her finger down the page looking for a month name.
look.prompt: Which job did Rosa skim for, and which did she scan for? How can you tell?

check.q: When you skim, what are you looking for?
choices: The general idea of the text
check.why: Skimming is fast reading for the big shape, not for one small fact.

check.q: The teacher asks how many eggs a queen lays in a day. What should you do?
choices: Scan for a number or the word eggs
check.why: Scanning hunts for one specific fact. You jump to the number or key word.

check.q: Which parts do you read when you skim?
choices: Title, headings, first sentences, last paragraph
check.why: Those parts give the shape of the text without reading it all.

lessons.title: Ask Before, During and After
lessons.mainIdea: Good readers ask questions before they read, while they read and after they finish, and then check whether the text answered them.
reading: Before Devon read the bee article, he looked at the title and asked, "Why is a hive like a city?" That question gave him a reason to read. It is a *before* question. Look at the title and the pictures. Ask what you already know. Ask what you want to find out.

While reading, keep asking. "Wait, what does colony mean?" "Why do the bees shiver?" "Does this fit with what the first paragraph said?" These *during* questions catch you when you drift. If you cannot answer a during question, stop and reread. That is not slow reading. That is smart reading.

After the last line, ask again. "Did I find out why a hive is like a city?" "What was the main idea?" "What surprised me?" If your before question never got answered, that is worth knowing too. It might be your next research question.

words.d: a large group of the same kind of animal living together, like all the bees in one hive
to read something again, often to fix a part that did not make sense

look.title: One Reader's Questions
look.text: Before: Why do bees dance? During: Is the figure eight the same as the waggle? Why does the sun matter to the dance? After: So the dance points toward the flowers, and the sun is the compass. I still do not know how far the flowers are. What tells them that?
look.cite: a reader's notes, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which of the reader's questions got answered? Which one could become a research question?

check.q: What is a good before question?
choices: What do I want to find out from this title?
check.why: Before questions come from the title and pictures and give you a reason to read.

check.q: You cannot answer a during question. What should you do?
choices: Ask a friend for the answer
check.why: Rereading fixes the part that did not make sense. That is what strong readers do.

check.q: The reader's before question never got answered. What does that tell her?
choices: It could be her next research question
check.why: An unanswered question is a place to keep looking, not a failure.

review.q: What is the difference between a topic and a main idea?
choices: A topic is a sentence; a main idea is a word
A topic is the subject; a main idea is the point made about it
A topic is always at the end
review.why: Topic: honeybees. Main idea: a hive works like a busy city.

review.q: In the class story, why was "every bee has a job" the main idea?
choices: Every other sentence was an example of it
review.why: The nectar, guard and queen sentences all held it up like table legs.

review.q: Which is a supporting detail for "A hive works like a city"?
choices: Guard bees stand at the door
review.why: Guards at the door is a job, which shows how the hive is like a city.

review.q: What is wrong with copying a sentence as your summary?
choices: Nothing; it is the best way
It does not show that you understood
review.why: A summary must be in your own words to prove you got the idea.

review.q: "Jamal checked his watch three times." What does this imply?
review.why: Checking a watch again and again is a clue that he is worried about being late.

review.q: Which part of a page gives you the meaning of a key term in the same sentence?
review.why: Writers bold a key term and often define it right there.

review.q: You need to find one date in a long article. Which is fastest?
review.why: Scanning hunts for one specific thing, like a number or a date.

review.q: Why ask a question before you read?
choices: It gives you a reason to read and something to look for
review.why: A before question turns reading into a search, which keeps you focused.

chapters.title: How a Text Is Built
chapters.bigQuestion: How does knowing the shape of a text help you understand and remember it?

story.title: Two Articles, One Tornado
story.kicker: One article tells what happened minute by minute. The other tells why the sky turned. Same storm, two shapes.
paragraphs: A tornado touched down west of a small Illinois town on a June afternoon. The next week, Ms. Okafor's class got two articles about it. "Read both," she said. "Then tell me how they are different." Priya read the first one. It felt like a movie.

The first article began at 3:10 p.m., when the sky went green. At 3:25 the sirens went off. At 3:40 the funnel touched a cornfield. At 3:52 it lifted. The article walked through the storm one minute at a time. Priya could almost hear the clock ticking.

The second article did not have a single clock time in it. It started with warm, wet air from the south. It said the warm air met cool, dry air from the north. The warm air rose, the storm began to spin, and the spin tightened into a funnel. Every sentence answered the question why.

"The first one is a sequence," Priya said. "First, next, then. The second one is cause and effect. This happens, so that happens." Ms. Okafor wrote both words on the board. "Two writers. Same tornado. Two shapes," she said.

Then she asked the class to take notes on each. For the first article, Priya drew a line with times on it. For the second, she drew arrows: warm air meets cold air, arrow, air rises, arrow, spin, arrow, funnel. Her notes looked like the articles. That was the whole point.
story.think: Priya's notes for each article had a different shape. Why would a line work for one and arrows for the other?

lessons.title: Sequence and Description
lessons.mainIdea: A sequence text tells events or steps in order, and a description text tells what something is like, feature by feature.
reading: Read this. "First, the sky turned green. Next, the sirens sounded. Then the funnel touched down. Finally, it lifted." Each event comes after the one before. This is a *sequence* text. Recipes, directions, and the story of a day are all sequences. Order is the whole point.

Now read this. "A tornado is a spinning column of air. It reaches from a storm cloud to the ground. It can be thin as a rope or wider than a town. Most last only a few minutes." Nothing happens in order here. Each sentence adds a feature. This is a *description* text. It tells what something is like.

How do you tell them apart? Ask, "Could I shuffle these sentences?" In a sequence, no. Mixing the order breaks it. In a description, mostly yes. The tornado is still a spinning column even if you read the width sentence first. Every text you read has a shape. Sequence and description are the first two.

words.d: a text shape that tells events or steps in time order
a text shape that tells what something is like, one feature at a time
the way a text is built or organized

look.title: Shuffle Test
look.text: Lake Michigan is the only Great Lake that lies entirely inside the United States. Its water is cold even in July. Its beaches in Chicago have soft sand. On a clear day the water looks blue-green near the shore.
look.prompt: Could you shuffle these sentences without breaking the paragraph? What shape is it?

check.q: Which shape puts events in time order?
check.why: Sequence means first, next, then. Order is the point.

check.q: "A tornado can be thin as a rope or wider than a town." What kind of sentence is this?
check.why: It tells what a tornado is like, one feature. That is description.

check.q: What does the shuffle test show?
choices: Sequence sentences can be mixed; description cannot
Description sentences can mostly be mixed; sequence cannot
Both shapes can be mixed freely
check.why: Mixing steps breaks a sequence. Mixing features usually leaves a description fine.

lessons.title: Compare and Contrast
lessons.mainIdea: A compare-and-contrast text shows how two things are alike and how they are different.
reading: "A tornado and a hurricane both spin. Both can flatten houses. But a hurricane is hundreds of miles wide and lasts for days. A tornado is usually less than a mile wide and lasts minutes." This paragraph holds two things side by side. That is *compare and contrast*.

To *compare* is to show what is the same. To *contrast* is to show what is different. Watch the words. "Both" and "also" and "alike" signal same. "But," "however," "while" and "unlike" signal different. Writers use these words like turn signals.

Try it on two things you know: a bus and a train. Both carry many people. Both have a driver. But a train runs on rails and a bus runs on streets. A train cannot turn to avoid traffic. When you can say both and but, you are thinking in this shape.

words.d: to show how two things are alike
to show how two things are different
a huge spinning storm that forms over warm ocean water and can last for days

look.title: Tornado and Hurricane Side by Side
look.cite: rounded, typical values chosen for this lesson; real storms vary a lot
look.prompt: Which numbers show a contrast? Name one way the two storms are alike that the table does not show.

check.q: What does contrast mean?
check.why: Contrast is difference. Compare is sameness.

check.q: Which word signals that two things are alike?
check.why: "Both" says two things share something. The others signal difference.

check.q: Which sentence is a contrast between a bus and a train?
choices: A train runs on rails, but a bus runs on streets
check.why: The "but" sentence shows a difference. The other three show sameness.

lessons.title: Cause and Effect
lessons.mainIdea: A cause-and-effect text explains why something happens: this cause leads to that effect.
reading: The second tornado article answered one question over and over: why? "Warm, wet air pushed north. Cool, dry air pushed south. Where they met, the warm air rose fast. Because the winds blew at different speeds, the rising air began to spin." Each sentence is a *cause* pushing an *effect*.

A cause is the reason. An effect is the result. Watch for "because," "so," "since," "as a result" and "led to." Also watch for chains. Warm air rising causes spin. Spin causes a funnel. The funnel causes damage. One effect becomes the next cause.

Here is a trap. Two things happening close together does not mean one caused the other. The sirens sounded, and then the funnel touched down. The sirens did not cause the tornado. Ask, "Did the first thing make the second thing happen?" If not, it is a sequence, not a cause.

words.d: the reason something happens
the result; what happens because of a cause
a line of causes and effects where each effect starts the next cause

look.title: Is It a Cause?
look.text: Read two pairs. Pair one: "The pond froze, so the ducks left." Pair two: "The bell rang, and then it started to snow." In the first pair, the freezing pond took away the ducks' food and swimming water. In the second, the bell and the snow just happened close in time.
look.prompt: Which pair is cause and effect? Which is only a sequence? How do you know?

check.q: In "the warm air rose, so the storm began to spin," what is the effect?
check.why: The spinning is the result. The rising warm air is the cause.

check.q: What is a chain of causes?
choices: Two things that happen at the same time
A line where each effect starts the next cause
check.why: Rising air causes spin, spin causes a funnel, the funnel causes damage. Each effect leads to the next.

check.q: The sirens sounded, then the funnel touched down. Did the sirens cause the funnel?
choices: No; they just happened close in time
Yes; the first thing always causes the second
check.why: Close in time is not the same as cause. The sirens did not make the tornado happen.

lessons.title: Problem and Solution
lessons.mainIdea: A problem-and-solution text names something wrong and then tells how people fixed it or could fix it.
reading: "Tornado sirens are loud, but people inside cannot always hear them. So the town added phone alerts. Now a warning buzzes in every pocket." First a *problem*. Then a *solution*. This shape shows up in science, history and the news all the time.

Watch for "problem," "trouble," "issue" and "the challenge was." Then watch for "solved," "fixed," "one answer" and "so they." Sometimes a text gives more than one solution. Sometimes it gives a solution that failed and then a better one. Keep track of which is which.

This shape is close to cause and effect, and students mix them up. Ask, "Is the writer telling me what went wrong and how to fix it?" That is problem and solution. "Is the writer telling me why something happens?" That is cause and effect. A problem is a kind of cause, but only one that someone tries to fix.

words.d: something wrong that needs to be fixed
a way to fix a problem

look.title: A Town Fixes a Problem
look.text: After the storm, the town had one shelter, and it was two miles from the school. Kids could never reach it in time. The school board voted to build a storm room inside the school itself. It has thick concrete walls and no windows. Now every student is thirty seconds from safety.
look.prompt: Name the problem and the solution. What words helped you find each?

check.q: "People could not hear the sirens, so the town added phone alerts." What shape is this?
check.why: Something was wrong (no one heard), and the town fixed it (phone alerts).

check.q: In the shelter story, what is the solution?
choices: The shelter was two miles away
A storm room inside the school
Kids could not reach the shelter
check.why: The storm room is the fix. The far-away shelter is the problem.

check.q: How is problem and solution different from cause and effect?
choices: Problem and solution has no reasons
Cause and effect only happens in stories
Problem and solution tells how something wrong gets fixed
check.why: Cause and effect explains why. Problem and solution adds a fix.

lessons.title: Words That Give Away the Shape
lessons.mainIdea: Signal words like first, both, because and solved tell you which structure a text is using before you finish it.
reading: Read just the first few words of a paragraph: "First, crack two eggs." You already know it is a sequence. "Unlike a frog, a toad..." Compare and contrast. "Because the river flooded..." Cause and effect. "The trouble with old bridges is..." Problem and solution. These are *signal words*. They give away the shape early.

Learn a few for each shape. Sequence: first, next, then, after, finally, dates and clock times. Description: for example, such as, looks like, is made of. Compare and contrast: both, also, alike, but, however, unlike. Cause and effect: because, so, since, as a result. Problem and solution: problem, trouble, so they, solved, one answer.

Signal words are clues, not proof. A description might use "first" just to start a list of features. So read a little more and check. If the sentences must stay in order, it is a sequence. If they explain why, it is cause and effect. The signal word points; the sentences tell.

words.d: a word or phrase that hints at how a text is organized, like first, but or because
a hint that helps you figure something out

look.title: Signal Words in the Two Tornado Articles
look.cite: counted for this lesson, in two model articles written for this course
look.prompt: Which counts point to sequence? Which point to cause and effect? Could you tell the shape from the counts alone?

check.q: A paragraph begins, "Because the river flooded..." Which shape is most likely?
check.why: "Because" signals a cause is coming.

check.q: Which set of words signals a sequence?
check.why: First, next and finally put events in order.

check.q: Why are signal words clues and not proof?
choices: A word like first can start a list of features, not just steps
check.why: Signal words point to a shape, but you must read on to be sure.

lessons.title: Notes That Match the Shape
lessons.mainIdea: Take notes in the shape of the text: a numbered list for sequence, a two-column chart for compare and contrast, arrows for cause and effect.
reading: Priya drew a line with times for the first article. She drew arrows for the second. Her notes matched the shape of each text. That is not a trick. It is the best way to remember. When your notes look like the text, your brain stores the ideas the way the writer built them.

Here is the plan. Sequence: a numbered list or a timeline. Description: a web, with the topic in the middle and features around it. Compare and contrast: two columns, or two circles that overlap. Cause and effect: boxes with arrows. Problem and solution: one box for the problem, one for each fix.

Try it with the shelter paragraph. Problem box: "Shelter two miles away; kids cannot reach it." Solution box: "Storm room inside school, concrete walls." Two boxes, ten words. You could tell the whole story from that. Notes that match the shape are short, and they stick.

words.d: a line with events marked on it in time order
a note shape with the topic in the middle and features drawn around it
a tall list; two columns side by side let you compare

look.title: Pick the Note Shape
look.text: Three students each read a different article. Amir's article explains why leaves turn red in fall. Beth's article compares two kinds of bridges. Carlos's article gives the steps to plant a tree. Amir draws two columns. Beth draws arrows. Carlos draws a web.
look.prompt: All three picked the wrong note shape. What should each student have drawn instead?

check.q: Which note shape fits a cause-and-effect text?
check.why: Arrows show one thing leading to another, which is what cause and effect does.

check.q: Beth's article compares two bridges. What should she draw?
check.why: Two columns put the two bridges side by side so she can compare and contrast.

check.q: Why do notes that match the shape help you remember?
choices: They store the ideas the way the writer built them
check.why: When your notes copy the structure, the ideas stick in that same order.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Texts
lessons.mainIdea: When two texts cover the same topic, compare what each one includes, what each leaves out, and how each is built.
reading: The two tornado articles covered the same storm. But they did not say the same things. The first had clock times and no reasons. The second had reasons and no clock times. Reading both, Priya knew more than she could learn from either one alone. That is why teachers give you two texts.

To compare two texts, ask three questions. What facts are in both? What facts are only in one? How is each text built? Make two columns. Put shared facts in the middle. Put the facts only in the first text on the left, and only in the second on the right.

Then ask why. Why did the first writer leave out the causes? Maybe she wanted readers to feel the minutes tick. Why did the second writer skip the clock? Maybe he wanted to teach the science. Each writer chose. Seeing the choice is the deepest kind of reading.

words.d: to put something in; a text includes the facts the writer chose to keep
to not put something in; every writer leaves out some facts

look.title: What Each Article Kept
look.text: Article 1 has: the sky turning green at 3:10, the sirens at 3:25, the funnel at 3:40, the lift at 3:52, the flattened barn. Article 2 has: warm wet air from the south, cool dry air from the north, rising air, winds at different speeds, the spin, the funnel, the flattened barn.
look.prompt: Which fact is in both articles? What is one thing you would know only from Article 2?

check.q: Why read two texts on the same topic?
choices: To learn more than either one alone gives
check.why: Each text includes different facts. Together they give a fuller picture.

check.q: Which fact was in both tornado articles?
check.why: Only the barn appears in both lists. The others are in just one article.

check.q: What is the deepest question to ask about two texts?
choices: Why did each writer choose to include what they did?
check.why: Seeing the writer's choices shows you the purpose behind each text.

lessons.title: The Author's Point and Reasons
lessons.mainIdea: An author often makes a point and gives reasons for it; your job is to find the point and check whether the reasons really hold it up.
reading: Some texts do more than tell. They argue. "Every school in Illinois should have a storm room. Tornadoes hit our state every year. Kids cannot reach a shelter two miles away. A storm room costs less than one school bus." The first sentence is the author's *point*. The next three are the *reasons*.

Find the point first. It is usually a sentence with "should," "must," "best" or "most important." Then find each reason. Ask, "Does this reason really hold up the point?" "Tornadoes hit every year" holds it up. "Storm rooms are painted gray" would not. A point with weak reasons is a weak point.

Then count. One reason is thin. Three good reasons with a fact for each is strong. Also notice what the author does not say. The storm-room author never mentions who pays. A careful reader sees the point, checks the reasons, and notices the hole.

words.d: the thing an author is trying to convince you of
a fact or idea an author gives to hold up a point

look.title: Find the Point
look.text: Chicago should plant more trees along its streets. Trees give shade, and shaded streets stay cooler in July. Tree roots soak up rain, so there is less water in the sewers after a storm. And a block with trees just looks like a place people care about.
look.prompt: What is the point? Which reason is the strongest, and which is the weakest? Why?

check.q: Which sentence is the author's point?
choices: Tornadoes hit our state every year
Every school in Illinois should have a storm room
A storm room costs less than a bus
Kids cannot reach a shelter two miles away
check.why: The point has "should" and is what the other sentences hold up.

check.q: Which reason would NOT hold up the storm-room point?
choices: Kids cannot reach the far shelter
It costs less than a bus
check.why: Paint color has nothing to do with whether schools need a storm room.

check.q: What hole does the careful reader find in the storm-room argument?
choices: It never says when tornadoes happen
It never says how big a storm room is
check.why: The author gives a cost but never says who would pay it.

lessons.title: Reading Science and History
lessons.mainIdea: A science text is usually built on causes, steps and diagrams, while a history text is built on dates, people and reasons, so read each with a different set of questions.
reading: A science text about tornadoes asks, "How does this work?" It is full of causes, steps and diagrams. Read it slowly. Check every diagram against the words. Ask, "Could I explain this to a friend with my hands?" If the text says warm air rises, picture it rising.

A history text about a tornado asks, "What happened to people, and why did it matter?" It has dates, names and places. It tells what people did before and after. Read it asking, "Who is telling this? What did they see? What changed because of it?"

One real storm, the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925, crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana and was one of the deadliest in United States history. A science text about it would explain the air and the spin. A history text would tell about the towns and the people who rebuilt. Same storm, different questions, different reading.

words.d: the story of what happened to people in the past
a text that explains how something in nature works
to build again after something was destroyed

look.title: Two Questions for One Storm
look.text: Imagine two books open on a desk. The left page shows a diagram: warm air, cold air, rising arrows, a spinning column. The right page shows a photo of a town's main street after the 1925 storm and a paragraph about neighbors sharing food. A student reads the left page with her hands moving. She reads the right page asking who these people were.
look.prompt: Which page is science and which is history? What question fits each one?

check.q: What question does a science text mostly answer?
check.why: Science texts explain how nature works, with causes, steps and diagrams.

check.q: Which parts would you expect most in a history text?
check.why: History tells what happened to people, so it is full of dates, names and places.

check.q: The Tri-State Tornado of 1925 crossed which three states?
check.why: It crossed Missouri, Illinois and Indiana, which is why it is called Tri-State.

lessons.title: Timelines and Steps
lessons.mainIdea: Timelines and numbered steps are sequences drawn out, so read them left to right or top to bottom and check the spacing between events.
reading: A *timeline* is a sequence you can see. Events sit on a line, earliest on the left, latest on the right. Priya's tornado timeline had 3:10, 3:25, 3:40 and 3:52. The spaces between the marks matter. The gap from 3:10 to 3:25 is fifteen minutes. From 3:40 to 3:52 is twelve. You can read time with your eyes.

Numbered *steps* are a sequence too. "1. Go to the lowest floor. 2. Get away from windows. 3. Cover your head." Read them in order. Do not skip. Step three makes no sense if you have not done step one. When steps have pictures, match each picture to its number before you move on.

Both tools can hide gaps. A timeline of a town might jump from 1925 to 1950. Ask what happened in between. A recipe might say "bake" without saying for how long. Good readers notice what a timeline or a list of steps leaves out, and they ask.

words.d: the parts of a task done one after another, usually numbered
a space or a missing part between two things

look.title: Minutes Between the Marks
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the clock times in the class story
look.prompt: Which gap was shortest? How long was the tornado on the ground?

check.q: On a timeline, where is the earliest event?
check.why: Timelines run left to right, earliest to latest.

check.q: Why should you read numbered steps in order?
choices: The numbers are the hard part
Later steps depend on earlier ones
The last step is always first
Order does not matter for steps
check.why: Step three makes no sense if step one is not done.

check.q: A timeline jumps from 1925 to 1950. What should a good reader do?
choices: Ask what happened in the gap
check.why: Timelines can leave things out. Noticing the gap is part of reading it.

review.q: The first tornado article walked through the storm minute by minute. What is its shape?
review.why: Events in time order with clock times is a sequence.

review.q: The second article explained why the storm formed. What is its shape?
review.why: Every sentence answered why, with one thing leading to the next.

review.q: Which shape can usually pass the shuffle test?
review.why: Features can be read in almost any order. Steps and causes cannot.

review.q: "Unlike a bus, a train runs on rails." What does "unlike" signal?
review.why: "Unlike" points to a difference between two things.

review.q: What is the best note shape for compare and contrast?
review.why: Two columns put two things side by side.

review.q: A writer gives a point and one reason. Another gives the same point with three reasons and a fact for each. Which argument is stronger?
choices: The one with three reasons and facts
review.why: More good reasons with facts hold up the point better.

review.q: What is the trap in cause and effect?
choices: Thinking two things close in time must be cause and effect
review.why: The sirens came before the funnel, but they did not cause it.

review.q: What happens when your notes match the text's shape?
choices: You do not need to read
The teacher writes them for you
review.why: Notes built like the text store the ideas the way the writer built them.

chapters.title: Charts, Sources and Research
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you find out something true that nobody in the room already knows?

story.title: The Yearbook in the Closet
story.kicker: A class wants to know when their school got its name. The answer is not online. It is in a dusty box.
paragraphs: Ms. Reyes's class had a question nobody could answer. "Why is our school called Harper Elementary?" Nate said it was named after a basketball player. Zoe said it was a mayor. The principal shrugged. "It was before my time." So the class decided to find out.

First they tried the internet. One website said the school opened in 1961. Another said 1958. A third had a picture of a totally different Harper school in another state. "Three answers," Ms. Reyes said. "That means we do not have one yet."

Then the librarian remembered a box in the closet. Inside were old yearbooks. The oldest was from 1959. On the first page was a photo of a woman in glasses and a note: "Our school is named for Dr. Alma Harper, who taught in this town for forty years." It was signed by the first principal.

"This is a primary source," Ms. Reyes said. "It was made at the time, by someone who was there." The websites were secondary. They were written later, by people who had never seen this page. Zoe wrote the fact in her notebook, in her own words, and wrote "Harper yearbook, 1959, page 1" beside it.

The class made a chart of every source they had used and how much they trusted each one. The yearbook went at the top. The website with the wrong school went at the bottom. Nate was a little sad it was not a basketball player. But now he knew something true that no one in the building had known.
story.think: Three websites gave three different answers. Why did the class trust the old yearbook more than any of them?

lessons.title: Reading a Chart or Graph
lessons.mainIdea: A chart or graph is a text made of shapes and numbers, so read its title, its labels and its key before you read its bars or lines.
reading: A bar *chart* about Harper Elementary shows five bars. The title says "Students at Harper by Year." The bottom says the years: 1960, 1980, 2000, 2020. The side says "number of students." The tallest bar is 1980. Without reading a sentence, you know the school was biggest in 1980.

Read a chart in this order. Title first: what is this about? Then the *labels* on the bottom and the side: what does each direction mean? Then the *key*, if there is one: what does each color stand for? Only then look at the bars or the line. Readers who skip to the bars often read the chart backward.

A line graph works the same way, but it shows change over time. A line going up means more. A line going down means less. A flat line means no change. Ask the same question you ask of a paragraph: "What is the main idea of this graph?" For the Harper chart, it is "The school grew, then shrank."

words.d: a picture that shows numbers with bars, lines or pieces
a word or number on a chart that tells what a part means
a small box on a chart or map that tells what each color or symbol means

look.title: Students at Harper by Year
look.cite: made-up numbers for a model chart, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What is the main idea of this chart in one sentence? Which year had the most students?

check.q: What should you read first on a chart?
check.why: The title tells what the chart is about. Then labels, then key, then bars.

check.q: On the Harper chart, which year had the most students?
check.why: 1980 has 520 students, the highest number.

check.q: A line on a graph goes down from left to right. What does that mean?
choices: The number is going down over time
check.why: On a line graph, down means less as time passes.

lessons.title: Tables and Maps
lessons.mainIdea: A table lines facts up in rows and columns, and a map shows where; both answer questions if you read their headings and their keys.
reading: A *table* is facts in a grid. The Harper class made one with three columns: Source, What It Said, and How Much We Trust It. Each *row* was one source. To find a fact, run your finger across a row and down a column until they meet. That box is your answer.

A map is a picture of a place from above. The class found a 1960 map of their town. The school was on it, but the big road next to it was not built yet. The key showed a small square for schools and a cross for churches. Read the title, the key and the compass. Then find what you need.

Both tables and maps answer questions fast. "Which source did we trust least?" Look at the trust column. "Was the school near the river in 1960?" Look at the map. A table or a map is a text. It just puts its sentences in boxes and pictures instead of lines.

words.d: facts arranged in rows and columns
one line across a table
the small symbol on a map that shows north, south, east and west

look.title: One Question, One Box
look.text: Picture the class's table. Row one: Harper yearbook, 1959. Row two: Town website. Row three: Website with the wrong school. The trust column says High, Medium, Low. Someone asks, "Which source got Medium?" A student runs her finger down the trust column, stops at Medium, then slides left to the source column.
look.prompt: Which source got a Medium rating? Describe the finger path you would use to find the yearbook's rating.

check.q: How do you find a fact in a table?
choices: Find where the right row and column meet
check.why: A table's answer sits in the box where a row and a column cross.

check.q: What does a map key tell you?
choices: The date the map was made
What each symbol or color means
check.why: The key explains the symbols, like a small square for a school.

check.q: The class map from 1960 did not show the big road. What does that tell you?
check.why: A map shows the place at the time it was made. The road came later.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source was made at the time by someone who was there; a secondary source was made later by someone who studied it.
reading: The 1959 yearbook was made in 1959, by people who were in the building. It is a *primary source*. A letter, a photo, a diary, a map from that year, a speech, a report card: all primary. They are the closest you can get to being there.

A website written last year about the school's history is a *secondary source*. So is an encyclopedia article or a textbook. The writer was not there. She read primary sources, or other secondary sources, and then wrote her own words. Secondary sources are useful. They gather a lot in one place. But they can pass along mistakes.

Here is the test. Ask, "Was this made at the time, by someone who saw it?" If yes, primary. If it was made later, by someone looking back, secondary. Both kinds have a place. Start with secondary sources to learn the big picture. Then check the facts against a primary source when you can.

words.d: something made at the time of an event by a person who was there
something made later by a person who studied the event
a book or website with short articles on many subjects

look.title: Two Sources, One Day
look.text: Source A: "Dear Mama, the new school opened today. Dr. Harper cut the ribbon herself. It rained but nobody cared." Source B: "Harper Elementary opened in the fall of 1959. The school was named for a local teacher. Its opening day drew a large crowd."
look.cite: written for this lesson: a letter from a student in 1959 and a website written years later
look.prompt: Which source is primary and which is secondary? What does the letter tell you that the website does not?

check.q: Which is a primary source about a school's opening in 1959?
choices: A letter written that day by a student
check.why: The letter was made at the time by someone who was there.

check.q: Why can secondary sources pass along mistakes?
choices: The writer was not there and relies on other sources
check.why: A writer who was not there can copy an error from another source.

check.q: What is a good order for using both kinds?
choices: Check primary sources first, then ignore the rest
Learn the big picture from secondary, then check facts with primary
check.why: Secondary sources give the overview. Primary sources let you check.

lessons.title: Fact or Opinion
lessons.mainIdea: A fact can be checked and shown true or false; an opinion is what someone thinks or feels, and it cannot be proved.
reading: "Harper Elementary opened in 1959." You can check that. You can find the yearbook and see. It is a *fact*. A fact can be true or false, but either way it can be checked. "Harper is the best school in town." Who says? How would you check it? That is an *opinion*.

Opinions often carry words like best, worst, should, beautiful, boring, and I think. Facts often carry numbers, dates and names. But be careful. "The school has the best test scores in the district" sounds like an opinion because of "best." It is really a fact, because scores can be checked.

Opinions are not bad. Writers are allowed to have them. The trouble comes when an opinion dresses up as a fact. "Everyone knows the old gym was better." Everyone? Ask, "Could I check this?" If the answer is no, you are holding an opinion, no matter how sure the writer sounds.

words.d: a statement that can be checked and shown to be true or false
what a person thinks or feels; it cannot be proved true or false

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: Four sentences from a school newsletter: "The new playground opened in April." "It has three slides and a climbing wall." "It is the most fun playground in Illinois." "Every kid should get extra recess to enjoy it." A student says two are facts and two are opinions.
look.prompt: Which two are facts and which two are opinions? What words gave the opinions away?

check.q: What makes a statement a fact?
check.why: A fact can be checked and shown true or false. Sounding sure is not enough.

check.q: "The school has the best test scores in the district." Fact or opinion?
choices: Fact, because scores can be checked
check.why: Even with "best," this can be checked against the real scores, so it is a fact.

check.q: Which sentence is an opinion?
choices: The playground is behind the gym
The playground is the most fun in Illinois
check.why: "Most fun" is a feeling. You cannot check it the way you can count slides.

lessons.title: Asking a Research Question
lessons.mainIdea: A good research question is specific, can be answered with sources, and is something you do not already know.
reading: Ms. Reyes's class started with a question: "Why is our school called Harper?" That is a good *research question*. It is specific. It can be answered by looking at sources. And nobody in the room knew the answer. If they had already known, there would be nothing to research.

Bad research questions come in two sizes. Too big: "What is the history of schools?" You could spend a lifetime on that. Too small: "What color is our school door?" Just go look. A good question sits in the middle. "When did our school get its gym, and why?" You could answer that in a week with a few sources.

Shape your question before you search. Start with a topic: our school. Ask what you wonder: who is it named for? Add a word that makes it specific: why. Then check: can a source answer this? Ms. Reyes says the best questions make you a little nervous, because you truly do not know.

words.d: looking carefully at sources to find out something true
exact and narrow, not vague or too big

look.title: Three Sizes of Question
look.text: Three students write research questions about Lake Michigan. Kim: "What is everything about Lake Michigan?" Dev: "Is Lake Michigan wet?" Sara: "Why did Chicago build a wall of rocks along the lake near our neighborhood?" Ms. Reyes reads all three and circles one.
look.prompt: Which question did she circle? What is wrong with each of the other two?

check.q: What makes "Why is our school called Harper?" a good research question?
choices: It is specific and can be answered with sources
check.why: It is narrow, sources can answer it, and nobody knew the answer yet.

check.q: What is wrong with "What is the history of schools?"
choices: It is too big to answer
It is about the wrong topic
check.why: That question could take a lifetime. A research question needs to be narrower.

check.q: "What color is our school door?" is a weak research question because...
choices: You can just go look; no research needed
check.why: A question you can answer by looking does not need research.

lessons.title: Notes in Your Own Words
lessons.mainIdea: Take research notes as short phrases in your own words, and put quotation marks around anything you copy exactly.
reading: Zoe read the yearbook note: "Our school is named for Dr. Alma Harper, who taught in this town for forty years." She did not copy it. She wrote: "named for Dr. Alma Harper, a teacher here 40 yrs." Short. Her words. That is a research *note*.

Why not copy? Two reasons. First, copying feels like learning but is not. Your hand moves and your brain sleeps. Second, when you write your report, copied notes turn into copied sentences. That is *plagiarism*, using someone's words as if they were yours. Notes in your own words keep you honest without trying.

Sometimes you want the exact words, like the yearbook's line signed by the first principal. Then copy it, put quotation marks around it, and write where it came from. Quotation marks are a promise: these words are not mine. Everything without marks is yours.

words.d: a short phrase you write down to remember a fact
using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own
the marks around words copied exactly from a source

look.title: The Same Fact, Three Ways
look.text: Source: "The gym was added in 1974 after the old one flooded twice in one spring." Note 1: "The gym was added in 1974 after the old one flooded twice in one spring." Note 2: "gym built 1974, old gym flooded 2x" Note 3: "the old one "flooded twice in one spring" (yearbook 1975, p. 3)"
look.prompt: Which note is a copy with no marks? Which is a good note in the student's own words? Which quotes honestly?

check.q: What is plagiarism?
choices: Using someone's words or ideas as if they were yours
Putting quotation marks around a quote
check.why: Plagiarism is passing off another person's words as your own.

check.q: Which is the best research note for the gym fact?
choices: I think the gym is nice
check.why: It is short, in the student's own words, and keeps the key facts.

check.q: You want to keep the exact words from a source. What must you do?
choices: Change one word so it is yours
Put quotation marks around it and note where it came from
check.why: Quotation marks plus the source is the honest way to keep exact words.

lessons.title: Keeping Track of Sources
lessons.mainIdea: Write down where every fact came from, with the title, the maker, the date and the page or web address, so you and your reader can find it again.
reading: Zoe wrote "Harper yearbook, 1959, page 1" next to her note. Two weeks later, when she wrote her report, she could say exactly where the fact came from. A friend who doubted her could go check. That is why researchers keep track of *sources*.

For each source, write four things. What is it called? Who made it? When was it made? Where did you find it: the page number, or the web address? For the yearbook: "Harper Elementary Yearbook, Harper students, 1959, page 1." For a website: its name, who runs it, the date if you can find it, and the address.

Keep a *source list* on one page. Number each source. Then in your notes, just write the number: "named for Dr. Harper (1)." At the end of your report, print the list. Readers can see you did real work. And if two sources disagree, you know exactly which said what.

words.d: any book, page, picture, person or website where a fact comes from
a numbered list of every source you used, with title, maker, date and place found
the line of letters at the top of a browser that names one page on the internet

look.title: Facts Found in Each Source
look.cite: counted for this lesson, from the class research in the chapter story
look.prompt: Which source gave the class the most facts? Why is it still worth listing the source that gave zero?

check.q: Why write down where a fact came from?
choices: So you or your reader can find and check it later
So you can skip taking notes
check.why: A source note lets anyone go back and check the fact.

check.q: Which four things go in a source entry?
check.why: Title, maker, date and page or address let a reader find the source again.

check.q: Two sources disagree about a date. How does a source list help?
choices: It picks the right date for you
It lets you see exactly which source said what
check.why: With numbered sources, you know which one gave each date and can check both.

lessons.title: A Solid Website or a Shaky One
lessons.mainIdea: Trust a website more when you can tell who made it, when it was made, and where its facts came from; trust it less when it hides those things or makes wild claims.
reading: The class found three websites. One was the town's own site, with the town seal, a date at the bottom, and a phone number. One was a page with no author, no date, and ads flashing everywhere. One had a photo of a different Harper school in another state. Which one would you trust?

Ask three questions. Who made this? A school, a library, a museum, a newspaper or a government office usually has people checking facts. A page with no name has no one to ask. When was it made? A page from ten years ago may be out of date. Where did the facts come from? A solid site tells you. A shaky one just says "trust me."

Watch for warning signs. Spelling mistakes in the title. Claims that sound too big: "the most famous school in America!" Pictures that do not match the words. Also check the site against another source. If the town site and the yearbook agree, you are on solid ground. If a lone site says something no one else says, be careful.

words.d: able to be trusted; a reliable source gets its facts right
old enough that some of the facts may have changed
something a writer says is true

look.title: Three Sites on the Screen
look.text: Site A: "Harper Elementary, official site of the Town of Millbrook. Updated this year. Contact: Town Clerk." Site B: "BEST SCHOOLS EVER!!! Harper opened in 1961 or maybe 1958. No author listed. Click here for free prizes." Site C: a school-history page from a library in another state, with a photo of a Harper High School and a note that it is in Ohio.
look.prompt: Rank the three sites from most to least reliable for the class's question. Give one reason for each rank.

check.q: Which sign makes a website MORE reliable?
choices: It names who made it and when
It says it is the best site ever
check.why: Knowing who made a page and when lets you judge and check it.

check.q: A page has no name and no date and says "trust me." What should you do?
choices: Be careful and check it against other sources
Trust it because it is online
check.why: A source that hides its maker and date needs checking before you use it.

check.q: Why was Site C not useful even though it came from a library?
choices: It was about a different Harper school in another state
check.why: A reliable site can still be about the wrong thing. Always check that it matches your question.

lessons.title: Putting the Answer Together
lessons.mainIdea: Research ends when you can state your answer in your own words, back it with your best sources, and say honestly what you still do not know.
reading: The class wrote its answer: "Harper Elementary is named for Dr. Alma Harper, a teacher who worked in our town for forty years. We know this from the 1959 yearbook, which was written by the first principal. The town website agrees." One sentence of answer. One sentence of source. One sentence of backup.

Notice what the class did not say. It did not say the school opened in 1961. Two websites disagreed, and the yearbook only showed 1959 or earlier. So they wrote, "The school opened in 1959 or a little before. We could not find the exact year." Saying "we could not find" is not failure. It is honesty, and it is what real researchers do.

Go back to the first question and answer it in one breath. Then list your sources. Then name what is still open. That open question, like "What year did it open?", is where the next research starts. Nate is already planning to ask the retired teacher who still lives on Elm Street.

words.d: the facts from sources that back up an answer
truthful; an honest researcher says what is known and what is not

look.title: One Class's Final Answer
look.text: Our school is named for Dr. Alma Harper, who taught here for forty years. Source: the 1959 yearbook, page 1, signed by the first principal. The town website agrees. We do not know the exact year the school opened; two websites give different dates, and no primary source we found gives one.
look.prompt: Which sentence is the answer? Which is the evidence? Which admits what is still unknown?

check.q: What three parts should a research answer have?
choices: A joke, a picture, a title
The answer, the sources, and what is still unknown
check.why: Answer, evidence and the open question make a complete, honest report.

check.q: Why did the class not state the opening year?
choices: The sources disagreed and no primary source gave it
check.why: Two websites gave different years and the yearbook did not settle it, so they said so.

check.q: What is the best thing to do with a question you could not answer?
choices: Leave it out of the report
Say it is unknown and make it the next research question
Pick the website with the nicest photos
check.why: Real researchers say what is open. Open questions are where the next search begins.

review.q: In the class story, why was the 1959 yearbook a primary source?
choices: It was the oldest book in the closet
It was made at the time by people who were there
review.why: A primary source is made at the time by someone who was there.

review.q: What should you read first on a chart?
review.why: The title tells what the chart is about. Then labels, then key, then bars.

review.q: "Harper is the best school in town." What is this?
review.why: "Best" is a feeling that cannot be checked, so it is an opinion.

review.q: Which research question is the right size?
choices: What color is the classroom door?
Why did our town build a new library in 2015?
review.why: It is specific, sources can answer it, and you cannot answer it just by looking.

review.q: You copy a sentence into your notes with no quotation marks and later use it in your report. What is that called?
review.why: Using someone's exact words as your own is plagiarism.

review.q: Which four things go in a source list entry?
choices: First word, last word, page count, font
review.why: Those four let a reader find the source again.

review.q: A website has no author, no date, and says "most famous school in America!" What is it?
choices: Shaky; check it against other sources
review.why: Missing maker and date plus a wild claim are warning signs.

review.q: The class could not find the exact opening year. What did they do?
choices: Said it was unknown and planned more research
Used the website with the wrong school
review.why: Honest research says what is known and what is still open.
